c: ADHD is supported by converging genetic, developmental, brain and treatment evidence. There is no single cause and no diagnostic brain or gene test — but the core machinery is well understood.

ADHD is one of the most studied conditions in psychiatry. Several independent lines of evidence point the same way: it is strongly heritable, it is linked to differences in how the brain develops, it involves the systems that regulate attention and motivation, and medicines that act on those systems reduce symptoms in trials.

Teaching model, not a diagnosis. Real systems involve hundreds of genes, many cell types and feedback loops. Solid = established mechanism · dashed = association in groups · dotted = hypothesis.

: Twin studies estimate heritability around 74%. Genome-wide studies find many common variants, each with a very small effect; 27 loci reached significance in the largest study, with 76 candidate genes enriched for expression in early brain development.
: Rare protein-truncating variants and copy-number changes add risk in some people. The 2023 study implicated SORCS3 through both common and rare variants.
: An estimated 84–98% of ADHD-influencing variants are shared with other psychiatric conditions — one reason ADHD so often co-occurs with others, and why genes cannot diagnose an individual.
: The enzyme that makes L-DOPA from tyrosine — the usual rate-limiting step in making dopamine and noradrenaline.
: Pumps dopamine from the cell fluid into storage vesicles, ready for release. Amphetamines disturb this storage and redistribute dopamine into the cell fluid.
: Recaptures released dopamine, ending its signal. Methylphenidate blocks it; amphetamines can reverse it so it pushes dopamine out.
: Recaptures noradrenaline — and in the prefrontal cortex, where DAT is sparse, much of the dopamine too. Atomoxetine blocks it.
: Enzymes that break dopamine and noradrenaline down inside and outside cells.
: Receive the dopamine signal. D2 receptors on the releasing cell also act as a brake (autoreceptors), feeding back to reduce release.
: Noradrenaline receptors in prefrontal cortex that strengthen task-relevant network signals. Guanfacine stimulates them.
: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine (→ noradrenaline in noradrenergic cells).
: Dopamine is packed into vesicles; unpacked dopamine is vulnerable to breakdown.
: Vesicles release their contents when the cell fires. Amphetamines add a second, firing-independent release route.
: Transporters pull the signal back in; enzymes break it down. Most medicines act by slowing clearance or forcing release.
: Autoreceptors and adaptation adjust the system over time. Transporter levels appear to shift after stimulant exposure — which complicates brain-scan comparisons.

: Prefrontal cortex regulates attention, behaviour and emotion; imaging shows these regions less active, with weaker connections, in ADHD on average. Its function depends on finely tuned dopamine and noradrenaline levels.
: In 223 children with ADHD versus 223 controls, half of cortical points reached peak thickness by about 10.5 years versus 7.5 years — a delay most marked in prefrontal regions.

: Across 23 sites, accumbens, amygdala, caudate, hippocampus and putamen were slightly smaller on average (effect sizes d −0.11 to −0.19), mainly in children; differences in adults were not significant. Medication did not explain them.

: In 53 unmedicated adults, PET showed lower dopamine transporter and D2/D3 receptor binding in reward regions, correlating with inattention. But a meta-analysis found transporter levels lower in drug-naive and higher in previously medicated people — so findings depend on history.
: Holding a goal, inhibiting distractions, switching and planning. Common-variant ADHD risk is associated with weaker performance on several executive measures.
: How strongly future or delayed outcomes drive effort now.
: Matching alertness to the task — too little or too much both degrade control.
: Knowing what to do and not being able to begin — one of the most commonly described ADHD difficulties.
: Losing track of a plan between deciding and doing; forgetting why you entered a room.
: Under-estimating elapsed time and time needed; 'now' and 'not now' as the only two clocks.
: Speech or action running ahead of evaluation.

— Common-variant risk is associated with midbrain dopaminergic neuron expression (Demontis 2023).
— Individual rare-variant routes are mostly untested.
— Whether transporter differences are a cause or an adaptation to past medication is unresolved (Fusar-Poli 2012).
Reward pathway markers → Reward and motivation:
— Individual differences in vesicle storage capacity shaping stimulant response is a research question, not an established ADHD mechanism.
: Blocks dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, so released transmitter stays active longer. First-line in children and one of two first-line options in adults (NICE).

: Enter the terminal, disturb vesicle storage and run transporters in reverse, releasing dopamine and noradrenaline independent of firing; they also block reuptake. In adults' clinician-rated trials, amphetamines had the largest average symptom effect, with lower tolerability than placebo.

: An inactive prodrug absorbed intact and converted to d-amphetamine, mainly by red blood cells. Same active drug as dexamfetamine, delivered more gradually — a different exposure profile, not an identical one.
: Non-stimulant that blocks the noradrenaline transporter, raising noradrenaline and prefrontal dopamine.
: Non-stimulant that stimulates alpha-2A receptors in prefrontal cortex, strengthening network signalling.
The useful way to think about it:
the parts are few, the regulation is complex.
Most people with ADHD do not have a broken part; they have many small differences in how parts are built and tuned, adding up across development.
